'''''Forsythia''''' {{IPAc-en|f|ɔr|ˈ|s|ɪ|θ|i|ə}}, {{IPAc-en|f|ɔr|ˈ|s|aɪ|θ|i|ə}}<ref>''Sunset Western Garden Book,'' 1995:606–607</ref> is a [[genus]] of [[flowering plant]]s in the olive [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] Oleaceae. There are about 11 [[species]], mostly [[native plant|native]] to [[Eastern Asia]], but one native to [[Southeastern Europe]].<ref name="zounds">{{Cite web|url=https://powo.science.kew.org/?name_id=369405|title=Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science|website=Plants of the World Online|access-date=2023-03-29|archive-date=2023-03-29|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230329175104/https://powo.science.kew.org/?name_id=369405|url-status=live}}</ref> ''Forsythia'' – also one of the plant's common names – is named after the [[botanist]] [[William Forsyth (horticulturist)|William Forsyth]].<ref name=foc>{{cite web|website=Flora of China|url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=112951|title=''Forsythia''|access-date=2007-11-20|archive-date=2022-10-30|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221030024455/http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=112951|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=fe>{{cite web |website=Flora Europaea |url=http://rbg-web2.rbge.org.uk/cgi-bin/nph-readbtree.pl/feout?FAMILY_XREF=&GENUS_XREF=Forsythia&SPECIES_XREF=&TAXON_NAME_XREF=&RANK= |title=''Forsythia'' |access-date=2007-11-20 |archive-date=2022-10-30 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221030024455/http://rbg-web2.rbge.org.uk/cgi-bin/nph-readbtree.pl/feout?FAMILY_XREF=&GENUS_XREF=Forsythia&SPECIES_XREF=&TAXON_NAME_XREF=&RANK= |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name=stabg>{{cite web|website=St Andrews Botanic Garden|url=http://www.st-andrews.ac.uk/~gdk/stabotanic/aprilpom.htm|title=Plant of the Month: ''Forsythia''|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070625173257/http://www.st-andrews.ac.uk/~gdk/stabotanic/aprilpom.htm |archive-date=2007-06-25}}</ref>

==Description==
''Forsythia'' are [[deciduous]] [[shrubs]] typically growing to a height of {{convert|1|-|3|m|0|abbr=on}} and, rarely, up to {{cvt|6|m|0}} with rough grey-brown bark. The leaves are borne oppositely and are usually [[Leaf shape|simple]], though sometimes trifoliate with a basal pair of small leaflets; they range between {{cvt|2|and|10|cm|in}} in length and, rarely, up to {{cvt|15|cm|in}}, with a margin that is serrated or entire (smooth). Twigs may be hollow or chambered, depending on the species.<ref>{{cite journal|title=The Forsythias|journal=Arnoldia|volume=10|date=14 April 1950|issue=2|url=http://arnoldia.arboretum.harvard.edu/pdf/articles/1950-10--the-forsythias.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150609155124/http://arnoldia.arboretum.harvard.edu/pdf/articles/1950-10--the-forsythias.pdf|url-status=dead|archive-date=June 9, 2015|author=Donald Wyman}}</ref>

The flowers are produced in the early spring before the leaves, bright yellow with a deeply four-lobed [[corolla (botany)|corolla]], the petals joined only at the base. These become pendent in rainy weather thus shielding the reproductive parts.
The fruit is a dry capsule, containing several winged seeds.<ref name=foc /><ref name=rhs>{{cite book|editor=Huxley, A.|year=1992|title=New RHS Dictionary of Gardening|publisher=Macmillan|isbn=0-333-47494-5}}</ref>

There is a long-standing belief that forsythia flowers produce [[lactose]], but lactose occurs only very rarely in natural sources other than milk, and attempts to find lactose in forsythia have been unsuccessful.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Toba, T.|author2= Nagashima, S. |author3= Adachi, S. |year=1991|title=Is lactose really present in plants?|journal=Journal of the Science of Food and Agriculture|volume=54|issue= 2 |pages=305–308 |doi=10.1002/jsfa.2740540217|bibcode= 1991JSFA...54..305T }}</ref>

The genus is named after [[William Forsyth (horticulturist)|William Forsyth]] (1737–1804), a Scottish [[botanist]] who was a royal head gardener and a founding member of the [[Royal Horticultural Society]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.eattheweeds.com/foraging-for-forsythia-2/|title=''Forsythia''|author=Green Deane|website=Eat the Weeds|date=31 August 2011|access-date=25 April 2013|archive-date=13 June 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130613023549/http://www.eattheweeds.com/foraging-for-forsythia-2/|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Species==
[[File:Green warming stripes.tif|thumb|An adaptation of the [[warming stripes]] that shows how the flowering time of ''[[Forsythia suspensa]]'' in [[Bavaria]] has changed between 1951 and 2020]]
The following species of ''Forsythia'' have been documented:<ref name=foc /><ref name=fe /><ref name=stabg /><ref name=rhs /><ref name=oxford>{{cite web|publisher=University of Oxford|website=Oleaceae information site |url=http://herbaria.plants.ox.ac.uk/fraxigen/fraxinus/oleaceae/forsythia.html |title=''Forsythia''}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www1.agric.gov.ab.ca/$department/deptdocs.nsf/all/opp4058?opendocument |title=Government of Alberta, Agriculture and Rural Development |access-date=2008-06-17 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150327000721/http://www1.agric.gov.ab.ca/$department/deptdocs.nsf/all/opp4058?opendocument |archive-date=2015-03-27 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=''Forsythia'' Vahl|url=http://www.worldfloraonline.org/taxon/wfo-4000014961|access-date=2021-05-05|website=www.worldfloraonline.org|archive-date=2021-01-09|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210109095649/http://www.worldfloraonline.org/taxon/wfo-4000014961|url-status=live}}</ref>{{overcite|date=April 2024}}
* ''[[Forsythia europaea]]'' <small>[[Árpád von Degen|Degen]] & [[Antonio Baldacci (botanist)|Bald.]]</small> – [[Balkans]] in [[Albania]] and [[Serbia]]
* ''[[Forsythia giraldiana]]'' <small>Lingelsh.</small> – northwest [[China]]
* [[Forsythia × intermedia|''Forsythia'' × ''intermedia'']] <small>[[Hermann Zabel|Zabel]]</small> – an artificial garden [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrid]] between ''F. suspensa'' and ''F. viridissima''<ref>{{Cite web|title=Forsythia × intermedia Zabel|url=http://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:608891-1|access-date=2021-04-04|website=Plants of the World Online|publisher=Kew Science|archive-date=2022-10-30|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221030024455/https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:608891-1|url-status=live}}</ref>
* ''[[Forsythia japonica]]'' <small>[[Tomitaro Makino|Makino]]</small> – [[Japan]]
* ''[[Forsythia koreana]]'' <small>([[Alfred Rehder|Rehder]]) [[Takenoshin Nakai|Nakai]]</small> – [[Korea]]
* ''[[Forsythia likiangensis]]'' <small>[[Ren-Chang Ching|Ching]] & K.M.Feng</small> – southwest China
* [[Forsythia × mandschurica|''Forsythia'' × ''mandschurica'']] <small>Uyeki</small> – northeast China
* ''[[Forsythia mira]]'' <small>M.C.Chang</small> – north central China
* ''[[Forsythia ovata]]'' <small>Nakai</small> – Korea
* ''[[Forsythia saxatilis]] '' <small>(Nakai) Nakai</small> – Korea
* ''[[Forsythia suspensa]]'' <small>([[Carl Peter Thunberg|Thunb.]]) [[Martin Vahl|Vahl]]</small> – eastern and central China
* ''[[Forsythia togashii]]'' <small>[[Hiroshi Hara (botanist)|H.Hara]]</small> – Japan ([[Shōdoshima]])
* ''[[Forsythia velutina]]'' <small>Nakai</small> – Korea
* ''[[Forsythia viridissima]]'' <small>[[John Lindley|Lindl.]]</small> – eastern China

A genetic study<ref name=kim>{{cite journal|author=Kim, K.-J. |year=1999|title=Molecular phylogeny of ''Forsythia'' (Oleaceae) based on chloroplast DNA variation|journal=P. Syst. Evol|volume=218|issue=1–2 |pages=113–123 |doi=10.1007/BF01087039 |bibcode=1999PSyEv.218..113K |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007%2FBF01087039|url-access=subscription}}</ref> does not fully match the traditionally accepted species listed above, and groups the species in four [[clade]]s: (1) ''F. suspensa''; (2) ''F. europaea—F. giraldiana''; (3) ''F. ovata—F. japonica—F. viridissima''; and (4) ''F. koreana—F. mandschurica—F. saxatilis''. Of the additional species, ''F. koreana'' is usually cited as a variety of ''F. viridissima'', and ''F. saxatilis'' as a variety of ''F. japonica'';<ref name=grin>{{cite web|website=Germplasm Resources Information Network |url=http://www.ars-grin.gov/cgi-bin/npgs/html/splist.pl?4734 |title=''Forsythia'' |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20000605122254/http://www.ars-grin.gov/cgi-bin/npgs/html/splist.pl?4734 |archive-date=2000-06-05}}</ref> the genetic evidence suggests they may be better treated as distinct species.

Forsythias are used as food plants by the [[larva]]e of some [[Lepidoptera]] species including the [[brown-tail]] and [[Gothic (moth)|Gothic moth]].{{cn|date=October 2024}}

==Garden history==
[[File:Forsythia suspensa 4090392 レンギョウ（連翹）.JPG|thumb|220px|left|Forsythia in full bloom]]
Two species of forsythia are at the heart of the selected forms and garden hybrids: ''Forsythia suspensa'' and ''F. viridissima''.  "These two species are, as it were, the founder-members of the forsythia family" writes [[Alice Margaret Coats|Alice Coats]]; they were the earliest species brought into Western gardens from the Far East and they have each played a role in the modern garden shrubs.<ref name='Coats'>{{cite book|last=Coats|first=Alice M.|title=Garden shrubs and their histories|year=1965|publisher=Dutton|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=byLxAAAAMAAJ&q=forsythia|access-date=2020-11-06|archive-date=2024-10-08|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241008223224/https://books.google.com/books?id=byLxAAAAMAAJ&q=forsythia|url-status=live}}</ref>

''Forsythia suspensa'', the first to be noticed by a Westerner, was seen in a Japanese garden by the botanist-surgeon [[Carl Peter Thunberg]], who included it (as a lilac) in his ''Flora Japonica'' 1784. Thunberg's professional connections lay with the [[Dutch East India Company]], and ''F. suspensa'' reached Holland first, by 1833. In England, when it was being offered by [[Veitch Nurseries]] in Exeter at mid-century, it was still considered a rarity. Not all the varieties of ''suspensa'' are splaying and drooping, best seen hanging over a retaining wall; an erect form found by Fortune near [[Peking]] in 1861 was for a time classed as a species—''F. fortunei''.<ref name="Coats" />

''Forsythia viridissima'', meanwhile, had overtaken it in European gardens. The Scottish plant-hunter [[Robert Fortune]] "discovered" it—in a mandarin garden of the coastal city of [[Zhoushan|Chusan]] (Zhoushan)—before he ever saw it growing wild in the mountains in [[Zhejiang]] province.<ref name="Coats" />
[[File:Goldglöckchen.JPG|thumb|''Forsythia'' × ''intermedia'' in Heidelberg, Germany]]
''Forsythia'' × ''intermedia'', as its name suggests, is a [[Hybrid (biology)#Hybrid plants|hybrid]] of ''F. suspensa'' and ''F. viridissima'', introduced in continental Europe about 1880. Repeated crosses of the same two parents have made reiterations of ''F. ''× ''intermedia'' quite variable. A [[bud sport]] of a particularly showy (''spectabilis'') form is widely marketed as ''F. ''× ''intermedia'' 'Lynwood Variety'.<ref name="Coats" /> This [[cultivar]] has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]],<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector – ''Forsythia'' × ''intermedia'' 'Lynwood Variety'|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/214902/Forsythia-x-intermedia-Lynwood-Variety/Details|access-date=7 June 2020|archive-date=8 October 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241008223226/https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/214902/forsythia-x-intermedia-lynwood-variety/details|url-status=live}}</ref> as have ''F. ''× ''intermedia'' Week End 'Courtalyn'<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector – ''Forsythia'' × ''intermedia'' Week End 'Courtalyn'|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/101339/Forsythia-x-intermedia-Week-End-Courtalyn/Details|access-date=7 June 2020|archive-date=6 July 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200706235718/https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/101339/Forsythia-x-intermedia-Week-End-Courtalyn/Details|url-status=live}}</ref> and ''F.'' Marée d'Or 'Courtasol'.<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector – ''Forsythia'' Marée d'Or 'Courtasol'|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/71890/Forsythia-Maree-d-Or-Courtasol/Details|access-date=7 June 2020|archive-date=6 July 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200706164323/https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/71890/Forsythia-Maree-d-Or-Courtasol/Details|url-status=live}}</ref>

About the time of the First World War further species were discovered by plant hunters in China: ''F. giraldian'' (found in Gansu, 1910) and ''F. ovata'' (collected from seed in Korea by [[Ernest Henry Wilson|E.H. Wilson]]) have been particularly useful as seed parents in 20th-century American crosses.<ref name="Coats" />

==Cultivation==
{{more citations needed|section|date=March 2020}}''Forsythia'' are early spring-flowering shrubs with yellow blooms,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/forsythia |title=Forsythia (Easter Tree, Forsythia, Golden Bells) |website=NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox |publisher=North Carolina State University |access-date=19 June 2023 |quote=Yellow flowers appear before foliage in February or March and last through April or May. |archive-date=4 April 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230404231622/https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/forsythia/ |url-status=live }}</ref> often seen in private gardens, public landscaping works and parks—notably during [[Eastertide]], when some of the plants are nicknamed ''Easter Tree'' in honor of the coming spring.<ref>{{cite web|title=Forsythia viridissima|url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/forsythia-viridissima/|access-date=2020-03-20|publisher=NCSU|language=en|archive-date=2020-03-27|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200327085114/https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/forsythia-viridissima/|url-status=live}}</ref> Two species/hybrids are commonly cultivated for ornamental use, ''[[Forsythia × intermedia]]'' and ''[[F. suspensa|F. suspensa]]''. They are grown in several climates and [[Hardiness zones|gardening zones]], prized for being tough and reliable [[perennial plants]]. ''F. × intermedia'' is the more commonly grown, smaller plant and has an upright habit with vivid flowers. ''F. suspensa'' is a large to very large shrub with paler blossoms, and can be grown in a weeping shape on banks. Many named garden cultivars can also be found. Budding ''Forsythia'' cuttings are frequently brought indoors, for their opening blooms, in the early spring.<ref name=rhs />

Vegetative [[plant propagation|propagation]] is usually achieved via [[Cutting (plant)|cuttings]], taken from green wood after flowering in late spring to early summer. Alternatively, cuttings may be taken between November and February, though this may reduce the flowering spectacle of the following spring.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/forsythia |title=Forsythia (Easter Tree, Forsythia, Golden Bells) |website=NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox |publisher=North Carolina State University |access-date=19 June 2023 |quote=Pruning should be done immediately after spring flowering; if done after mid-July, you will likely remove flower buds for the following spring. To rejuvenate an older plant, you can cut it back almost ground level. |archive-date=4 April 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230404231622/https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/forsythia/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Low-hanging boughs that touch the ground will often take root, adding to the total mass of the plant, but can be removed for transplanting. A common practice (known as [[layering (horticulture)|layering]]) is to place a weight over a branch to keep it on the ground and, after it has rooted, to dig up the roots and cut the rooted part from the main branch; this can then be planted.

==Uses==

===Medicinal use===
''[[Forsythia suspensa]]'' is considered one of the 50 fundamental herbs in [[Chinese herbology]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Forsythia Lian Qiao Weeping PFAF Plant Database|url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/forsythia-viridissima/|first=Thunb|last=Vahl|date=2019-05-02|publisher=Plants for a Future|language=en|access-date=2020-03-27|archive-date=2020-03-27|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200327085114/https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/forsythia-viridissima/|url-status=live}}</ref>
Forsythia fruits find use in [[traditional Chinese medicine]] in the treatment of [[bacterial infections]] and [[Upper respiratory tract infection|upper respiratory disease]], by virtue of their [[antipyretic]] and [[anti-inflammatory]] properties. When used for these purposes, they are combined with other herbs - most notably with the flowers of certain species of ''[[Lonicera]]'' (honeysuckle). Furthermore, the fruits are also employed as a [[diuretic]] and as a '[[Cardiovascular system|cardiovascular]] tonic'. The species involved in such use are ''Forsythia suspensa'', ''F. koreana'', and ''F. viridissima''.<ref>Drugs.com https://www.drugs.com/npp/forsythia.html Retrieved at 11.51 on Friday 2025-3-14.</ref>

===Musical instrument===
Forsythia sticks are used to [[Bow (music)|bow]] a Korean stringed instrument called an ''[[ajaeng]]''.<ref>{{cite web|title=Ajaeng|url=https://www.culturecontent.com/content/contentView.do?search_div=CP_THE&search_div_id=CP_THE008&cp_code=cp0225&index_id=cp02250025&content_id=cp022500250001&print=Y|publisher=Culture Content|access-date=2020-03-20|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180414233909/https://www.culturecontent.com/content/contentView.do?search_div=CP_THE&search_div_id=CP_THE008&cp_code=cp0225&index_id=cp02250025&content_id=cp022500250001&print=Y|archive-date=2018-04-14|language=ko}}</ref>

==Common names==
In some regions, the plant may be known as '''Easter tree''' and the flowers as ''yellow bells''.{{citation needed|date=October 2020}} In Iran, the plant is known as "yellow Jasmine".
